content: Before administering misoprostol tablets, it is crucial to ensure they are stored properly, as they degrade when exposed to humidity. Antenatal distribution programs for misoprostol can be enhanced by implementing community awareness campaigns or other educational measures to inform pregnant women and their families about the importance of this medication. Programs aimed at using uterotonics for the prevention of postpartum hemorrhage (PPH) should ensure that women are adequately informed beforehand. This includes educating them about the necessity of uterotonics for PPH prevention, the available options, potential side effects, and their right to make informed decisions about their care. Women should also be made aware of the risks associated with misoprostol use during pregnancy and labor, particularly before the baby is born. In regions with high rates of unexpected multiple pregnancies, it is essential to ensure that misoprostol is not administered before the delivery of a second twin. This can be achieved by administering the drug only after the placenta has been expelled. Recommendations should be tailored to suit the specific needs of different countries and healthcare systems. Any modifications to these recommendations must be explicitly justified and transparently documented. The implementation of advance misoprostol distribution programs for PPH prevention requires addressing several knowledge gaps through primary research. Key questions include the benefits and harms of advance misoprostol distribution, the comparative effectiveness of different distribution strategies, and the impact of introducing such programs on maternal and perinatal health outcomes, as well as healthcare utilization. Barriers to the effective implementation and scaling up of these recommendations may arise from patient behaviors, healthcare provider practices, or the organization of care. These barriers include a lack of understanding of misoprostol's value in preventing PPH, insufficient trained personnel, safety concerns regarding misoprostol misuse, inadequate systems for monitoring its distribution and use, and ineffective referral mechanisms for women requiring additional care. Strategies to address these barriers include integrating the recommendations into existing antenatal care packages, particularly in settings where skilled birth attendants may not be available. Monitoring and evaluation of the implementation process should be conducted at health service, country, and regional levels. This includes tracking the coverage of prophylactic uterotonics as a process indicator for PPH prevention and assessing the return of unused misoprostol tablets as a measure of retrieval strategy success. The WHO has developed specific guidance for evaluating the quality of care for severe maternal complications, including PPH, using near-miss and criterion-based clinical audit concepts. Monitoring the quality of uterotonic drugs in low-resource settings can help healthcare providers select the most effective options for PPH prevention. The recommendation will be reviewed annually by the WHO Executive Guideline Steering Group to prioritize updates based on new evidence. If no new evidence emerges, the recommendation may be revalidated. Any concerns about the validity of the recommendation should be promptly communicated to guideline implementers, along with plans for updates. WHO welcomes suggestions for additional questions to be included in future updates.
